docs.title: Installation & Setup
docs.text: This guide explains how to install and run MemoraDB, either by downloading a pre-built release package or building from source.

docs.title: Pre-Built Binaries (Recommended for Users)
docs.text:
If you just want to run MemoraDB without compiling code:

  1. Go to the GitHub Releases page.
  2. Download the pre-packaged archive for your operating system:
  3. Windows: MemoraDB-windows-x64.zip
  4. Linux: MemoraDB-linux-x64.tar.gz
  5. macOS: MemoraDB-macos-universal.tar.gz
  6. Extract the downloaded archive to any folder on your machine.
  7. Open your terminal in that folder and run the executable:
  8. On Windows: .\memora.exe
  9. On Linux/macOS: ./memora

[!TIP] Zero Extra Setup Required: All necessary runtime libraries (including ONNX Runtime) and the default neural embedding model are fully pre-packaged inside the release archive. You do not need to install Python, external vector databases, or any auxiliary services.

docs.title: Building from Source (For Developers)
docs.text: Building MemoraDB from source gives you full access to the codebase, build flags, and developer test suite.

docs.title: 1. Install Prerequisites
docs.text:
Ensure you have a C++17 compatible compiler, Git, CMake, and Ninja installed:

WindowsLinux (Ubuntu / Debian)macOS

You can quickly install the required tools using winget in PowerShell:

# Install CMake and Ninja
winget install --id Kitware.CMake -e
winget install --id Ninja-build.Ninja -e

For the C++17 compiler, you can use either: * Visual Studio 2022 with the "Desktop development with C++" workload, or * MinGW-w64 (e.g., via MSYS2: pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc).

Install the build essentials, CMake, Git, and Ninja via apt:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git cmake ninja-build build-essential

Install tools using Homebrew:

brew install git cmake ninja

docs.title: 2. Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Clone the MemoraDB repository from GitHub:

git clone https://github.com/v1haan24/MemoraDB.git
cd MemoraDB

docs.title: 3. Compile the Database
docs.text:
You can compile with Ninja (fastest) or without Ninja using standard Makefiles:

With Ninja (Recommended)Without Ninja (MinGW / Make) 
# 1. Configure build directory
cmake -G "Ninja" -S . -B build

# 2. Compile Release binary
cmake --build build --config Release

# 3. Launch MemoraDB
# On Windows:
.\build\memora.exe
# On Linux / macOS:
./build/memora

# On Windows (MinGW):
cmake -G "MinGW Makefiles" -S . -B build
cmake --build build --config Release
.\build\memora.exe

# On Linux / macOS (Unix Makefiles):
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
./build/memora

docs.title: 4. Running the Developer Test Suite (Optional)
docs.text:
MemoraDB includes an automated unit and integration test suite powered by GoogleTest and CTest. Tests are disabled by default during normal builds and can be enabled with -DMEMORA_BUILD_TESTS=ON:

# Configure and build tests
cmake -G "Ninja" -S . -B build-tests -DMEMORA_BUILD_TESTS=ON
cmake --build build-tests

# Run all tests
ctest --test-dir build-tests --output-on-failure

For detailed test suite documentation, test filters, and architectural testing details, see the Testing Guide.

docs.title: Why 64-Bit Architecture is Required
docs.text:
MemoraDB requires a 64-bit operating system (x86_64 / AMD64 or ARM64):

  1. Precompiled ONNX Runtime Engine: Microsoft distributes modern pre-built ONNX Runtime C++ release binaries exclusively for 64-bit platforms (win-x64, linux-x64, osx-universal2). There are no 32-bit builds available.
  2. Dense Vector Memory Space: In-process inference and vector indexes process 384-dimensional floating-point tensors (float[384] = 1,536 bytes per semantic row). Managing large vector candidate sets in memory requires a 64-bit virtual address space.
  3. 64-Bit Disk Offsets & Timestamps: The binary storage engine uses 64-bit unsigned integers (uint64_t) for file byte seek offsets and millisecond epoch timestamps, ensuring continuous durability without 32-bit integer overflow limits.

docs.title: Verifying the Installation
docs.text:
Launch the executable from your terminal:

# Windows
.\build\memora.exe

# Linux / macOS
./build/memora

Verify the status indicators printed below the startup banner:

  ●  temporal engine ready              ●  append-only storage ready
  ●  semantic vector search ready        ●  embedding model ready
  • All green dots (●) indicate that storage, temporal indexing, and semantic embedding inference are fully initialized.
  • Type .about to verify database version information.
  • Type .exit or .quit to leave the REPL.

docs.title: Quick Start Guide
docs.text: Get up and running with MemoraDB in 5 minutes. This tutorial guides you from launching the REPL to running your first relational, temporal, and semantic queries.

docs.title: 1. Start the MemoraDB Shell
docs.text:
Launch the executable from your terminal:

.\build\memora.exe

You are greeted by the interactive prompt:

memora>

[!NOTE] All SQL statements in MemoraDB must end with a semicolon (;). Statements can span multiple lines. REPL meta-commands begin with a dot (.) and do not use semicolons.

docs.title: 2. Create Your First Table
docs.text:
Let's create a table named documents with an integer primary key, a category string, and a semantic text body:

CREATE TABLE documents (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    category STRING(30),
    content STRING(300) SEMANTIC
);

Expected Output: 

Created table 'documents' (3 columns) with semantic index

docs.title: 3. Insert Initial Records
docs.text:
Insert three records using positional column order:

INSERT INTO documents VALUES (1, "Databases", "Relational databases use tables, rows, and B-tree indexes.");
INSERT INTO documents VALUES (2, "DevOps", "Kubernetes automates container deployment, scaling, and operations.");
INSERT INTO documents VALUES (3, "Artificial Intelligence", "Large language models generate text based on neural transformer architectures.");

Expected Output: 

1 row inserted
1 row inserted
1 row inserted

During each insert into a table with a SEMANTIC column, MemoraDB generates a 384-dimensional embedding vector in-process using the MiniLM model and appends it to data/documents/documents.vec.

docs.title: 4. Query Current Data
docs.text:
Retrieve all records:

SELECT * FROM documents;

Filter by an exact match on a column:

SELECT id, category FROM documents WHERE id = 2;

docs.title: 5. Perform Semantic Vector Search
docs.text:
Search for concepts even if the exact keywords are not present:

SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "orchestrating docker containers" LIMIT 3;

Result: Row 2 ("Kubernetes automates container deployment...") is returned at the top of the results with a high cosine similarity score, despite not containing the word "docker".

docs.title: 6. Update a Record and Observe Versioning
docs.text:
Update row 1:

UPDATE documents SET content = "Relational databases support SQL queries and transactional ACID guarantees." WHERE id = 1;

Now inspect the complete historical timeline for row 1:

HISTORY documents WHERE id = 1;

You will see two versions of row 1: the original record from step 3 and the updated record from step 6, each marked with its creation timestamp.

docs.title: 7. Query Past State with AS OF
docs.text:
Query how row 1 looked before the update:

SELECT * FROM documents AS OF 2026-01-01 WHERE id = 1;

If the timestamp provided is before the row existed, no record is returned. If you supply the timestamp corresponding to the first insert, the original version is returned!

docs.title: 8. Useful REPL Commands
docs.text:
Try out the REPL utilities:

  • .tokens SELECT * FROM documents; — Inspect how the lexer tokenizes your statement.
  • .history — Display your shell command history.
  • .help SELECT — Display the precise grammar rules for SELECT.
  • .clear — Clear the terminal screen.
  • .exit — Exit the MemoraDB shell.

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text: This page details the software, hardware, and runtime requirements for compiling and running MemoraDB.

docs.title: Hardware Requirements
docs.text: Component Minimum Recommended Architecture 64-bit x86 (x86_64 / AMD64) or Apple Silicon (arm64 via universal binary) 64-bit x86_64 with AVX2 instruction support CPU 2 cores 4+ cores (accelerates ONNX embedding inference) RAM 2 GB 4 GB+ (to accommodate the MiniLM model in memory) Disk Space 500 MB free space 2 GB+ (for build cache, ONNX runtime, and model assets)

docs.title: Operating System Support
docs.text:
MemoraDB's CMake configuration includes automatic platform detection and FetchContent hooks for the following 64-bit operating systems:

  • Windows: Windows 10, 11, or Windows Server (x86_64).
  • Linux: Modern Linux distributions (Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+, Fedora 36+, Arch Linux) with glibc 2.31+ on x86_64.
  • macOS: macOS 11 (Big Sur) or newer on Intel or Apple Silicon (universal2 ONNX archive supported).

[!NOTE] 32-bit platforms (e.g., x86 32-bit, ARM32) are explicitly not supported by the automatic ONNX Runtime download script in CMakeLists.txt.

docs.title: Build Prerequisites
docs.text: To compile MemoraDB from source, ensure the following tools are installed and present in your system PATH:

docs.title: 1. C++ Compiler (C++17 Support Required)
docs.text:
MemoraDB strictly relies on ISO C++17 language features (std::variant, std::optional, std::filesystem, structured bindings, and inline variables).

  • Windows: Visual Studio 2019 / 2022 (MSVC v142/v143) with the C++ Desktop Development workload, or MinGW-w64 (GCC 9+).
  • Linux: GCC 9.0+ or Clang 10.0+.
  • macOS: Xcode Command Line Tools 12.0+ (Apple Clang).

docs.title: 2. CMake
docs.text:
• Version: CMake 3.20 or higher is required (cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)).
  • Verification: 
    cmake --version

docs.title: 3. Build Generator
docs.text:
• Ninja (Recommended for fast incremental builds on all platforms): 
    ninja --version
  • Alternatively, Visual Studio Solution generators on Windows or GNU Make on Linux.

docs.title: 4. Network Access (Build-Time Only)
docs.text:
During the initial CMake configure phase, CMake will automatically download: 1. Microsoft ONNX Runtime 1.22.0: * Windows: onnxruntime-win-x64-1.22.0.zip (~45 MB) * Linux: onnxruntime-linux-x64-1.22.0.tgz (~55 MB) * macOS: onnxruntime-osx-universal2-1.22.0.tgz (~50 MB) 2. Hugging Face Model Assets (sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2): * model.onnx (~86 MB) * vocab.txt (~232 KB)

If you are working in an air-gapped or offline environment, you must manually populate ONNXRUNTIME_ROOT and the model directory prior to configuring CMake.

docs.title: Runtime Requirements
docs.text:
When executing memora (or memora.exe on Windows):

  1. Shared Libraries:
  2. On Windows: onnxruntime.dll and onnxruntime_providers_shared.dll must be in the same folder as memora.exe (the build system automatically copies them post-build).
  3. On Linux/macOS: The ONNX dynamic libraries must be in the executable directory or discoverable via LD_LIBRARY_PATH / DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH.
  4. Model Assets:
  5. The directory models/all-MiniLM-L6-v2/ containing model.onnx and vocab.txt must reside adjacent to the executable. The executable dynamically locates this directory relative to its own binary path using platform-specific APIs (_get_pgmptr on Windows, /proc/self/exe on Linux, and _NSGetExecutablePath on macOS).
  6. Data Directory:
  7. MemoraDB creates and manages a local data/ directory relative to the current working directory from which you launch the REPL. Ensure write permissions exist in that directory.

docs.title: CLI & REPL Reference
docs.text: The MemoraDB interactive shell (REPL) provides an environment for executing SQL queries, inspecting lexer tokens, reviewing command history, and monitoring database engine status.

docs.title: Meta-Commands vs. SQL Statements
docs.text:
The shell distinguishes between two classes of input:

  • SQL Statements: Parsed by the SQL compiler, must terminate with a semicolon (;), and operate on database tables.
  • Meta-Commands: Begin with a dot (.), do not use a semicolon, and control shell behavior.

docs.title: Supported Meta-Commands
docs.text:
Command Arguments Description .help [topic] Displays general shell help, or detailed syntax for a specific SQL command or concept (e.g., .help SELECT, .help WHERE, .help DATE). .tokens <statement> Passes a statement through the lexer and prints a table of token types, line numbers, column offsets, and token values. .history (none) Prints all SQL statements and meta-commands entered during the current session. .clear / .cls (none) Clears the terminal screen. .about (none) Displays the project summary, core architectural features, and official GitHub repository link. .exit / .quit / .q (none) Closes the database catalog and exits the REPL.

[!NOTE] Bare exit and quit (without a leading dot) are also accepted as aliases to exit the shell.

docs.title: 1. .help [topic]
docs.text:
Without arguments, .help prints a summary of commands. When passed a topic name, it displays detailed syntax and examples:

memora> .help SELECT
SELECT
Syntax:
  SELECT * | <col1>[, <col2> ...]
  FROM <table>
  [AS OF <date> | SNAPSHOT <date> | BETWEEN <date1> AND <date2>]
  [WHERE <condition>]
  [ORDER BY <col> [ASC|DESC]]
  [LIMIT <n>];

Notes:
  WHERE and the temporal clause can appear in either order.
  SIMILAR TO is supported only on SEMANTIC columns.

Examples:
  SELECT * FROM notes;
  SELECT id, body FROM notes AS OF 2026-09-20 WHERE id = 1;
  SELECT * FROM notes WHERE body SIMILAR TO 'database search' LIMIT 5;

Supported Topics: CREATE, DROP, DESCRIBE, SHOW, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT, WHERE, SIMILAR, AS OF, ORDER BY, LIMIT, COMPARE, EVOLUTION, HISTORY, ROLLBACK, COMPACT, DATE, TYPES, CLEAR.

docs.title: 2. .tokens <statement>
docs.text:
The .tokens command exposes the internal lexical analysis pipeline. It tokenizes the input string without executing it and displays each token with syntax coloring:

memora> .tokens SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id = 1;
#    type                line:col  value
0    SELECT              1:1       SELECT
1    STAR                1:8       *
2    FROM                1:10      FROM
3    IDENTIFIER          1:15      notes
4    WHERE               1:21      WHERE
5    IDENTIFIER          1:27      id
6    EQUAL               1:30      =
7    INTEGER_LITERAL     1:32      1
8    SEMICOLON           1:33      ;
9    END_OF_FILE         1:34      
Tokens: 10 (0.142 ms)

docs.title: 3. .history
docs.text:
Prints the chronological list of commands executed in the current REPL session:

memora> .history
1  CREATE TABLE notes (id INT PRIMARY KEY, content STRING(200) SEMANTIC);
2  INSERT INTO notes VALUES (1, "MemoraDB temporal test");
3  SELECT * FROM notes;

docs.title: Terminal Features
docs.text:
• Truecolor & 256-Color Gradients: The REPL automatically detects 24-bit TrueColor (COLORTERM=truecolor) and ANSI-256 terminals, rendering a full-color banner on launch.
  • Interactive Diagnostic LEDs: Displays real-time status indicators for the temporal engine, append-only storage, vector index, and ONNX model.
  • Console Title: Sets the terminal emulator window title to "MemoraDB".
  • Signal Handling: Catches SIGINT (Ctrl+C) gracefully to prevent database file corruption during active writes.

docs.title: Data Types Reference
docs.text: MemoraDB is a strongly-typed database system. All table columns must be declared with one of four supported data types during CREATE TABLE.

docs.title: Supported Types
docs.text: Type C++ Representation Binary Size Permitted Literals Description INT int32_t 4 bytes 42, -10, 0 32-bit signed integer. FLOAT float 4 bytes 3.14, -0.05, 100.0 IEEE 754 single-precision floating point. STRING(n) char[n] n bytes 'text', "text" Fixed-width string buffer of size n. Requires explicit size. BOOL uint8_t 1 byte true, false 8-bit boolean flag (0 = false, 1 = true).

docs.title: 1. INT
docs.text:
• Range: -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647.
  • Supports unary minus (-) in SQL queries.
  • Comparison operators supported: =, !=, <, <=, >, >=.
  • Sorting: Numerically ordered.

docs.title: 2. FLOAT
docs.text:
• Precision: ~7 decimal digits of precision.
  • Supports unary minus (-) in SQL queries.
  • Comparison operators supported: =, !=, <, <=, >, >=.
  • Sorting: Numerically ordered.

docs.title: 3. STRING(n)
docs.text:
• Mandatory Size: Must be declared with an explicit capacity, e.g., STRING(50).
  • Storage: Fixed-size buffer on disk. Strings shorter than n bytes are null-padded; strings longer than n are rejected during validation.
  • Quoting: Can be enclosed in single quotes ('...') or double quotes ("...").
  • Comparison operators supported: =, !=, <, <=, >, >= (lexicographical).
  • Special Modifier: Can be marked with SEMANTIC to enable AI vector search.

docs.title: 4. BOOL
docs.text:
• Accepted values: true or false (case-sensitive literal strings).
  • Comparison operators supported: = and != only. Ordering operators (<, <=, >, >=) evaluate to false.
  • Sorting: false precedes true in ascending order.

docs.title: Column Modifiers
docs.text: Columns can be annotated with modifiers during CREATE TABLE:

docs.title: PRIMARY KEY
docs.text:
• Constraint: Exactly one column per table must be designated PRIMARY KEY.
  • Immutability: The primary key value cannot be modified via UPDATE.
  • Indexing: Automatically indexed in-memory by HistoryIndex.
  • Valid Types: Any supported type (INT, STRING, FLOAT, BOOL).

docs.title: SEMANTIC
docs.text:
• Constraint: Valid only on STRING columns.
  • Vector Model: Generates a 384-dimensional vector embedding for the text using all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
  • Storage: Vector embeddings are saved to a dedicated .vec file and indexed by VectorIndex.
  • Querying: Enables the SIMILAR TO operator in SELECT statements.

docs.title: Identifier Naming Limits
docs.text:
MemoraDB enforces fixed buffer sizes for schema identifier names in metadata headers:

Identifier Type Constant Constant Name Buffer Size Maximum Character Length Table Name tns Table Name Size 30 bytes 29 characters (+ 1 null terminator \0) Column Name cns Column Name Size 30 bytes 29 characters (+ 1 null terminator \0)

[!NOTE] Names exceeding 29 characters are rejected by the catalog validation logic during CREATE TABLE. Identifiers must start with an alphabetic character or underscore (_).

docs.title: Formal Grammar & Syntax Notation
docs.text: This page defines the notation conventions used throughout the MemoraDB documentation and provides the complete formal Extended Backus-Naur Form (EBNF) grammar for the MemoraDB SQL dialect.

docs.title: Syntax Notation Guide
docs.text:
The command reference pages in this documentation use standard typographical conventions to describe SQL syntax:

Symbol Meaning Example Explanation <...> Placeholder <table>, <column> Replace this token with your own table name, column name, or literal value. [ ... ] Optional element [WHERE <condition>] The enclosed clause or keyword may be included or omitted. \| Alternative / Choice ASC \| DESC Choose exactly one of the listed options. * Zero or more ColumnDef ( "," ColumnDef )* The preceding element may repeat zero or more times separated by commas. + One or more Digit+ The preceding element must appear at least once. UPPERCASE SQL Keyword SELECT, FROM, WHERE Keywords must be written as shown (case-insensitive in MemoraDB).

docs.title: EBNF Specification
docs.text:
(* Top-level Program *)
Program               ::= Statement*

Statement             ::= ( CreateTableStmt
                          | DropTableStmt
                          | DescribeTableStmt
                          | ShowTablesStmt
                          | InsertStmt
                          | UpdateStmt
                          | DeleteStmt
                          | SelectStmt
                          | CompareStmt
                          | EvolutionStmt
                          | HistoryStmt
                          | RollbackStmt
                          | CompactStmt ) ";"

(* DDL Statements *)
CreateTableStmt       ::= "CREATE" "TABLE" Identifier "(" ColumnDef ( "," ColumnDef )* ")"
ColumnDef             ::= Identifier DataType ( Modifier )*
Modifier              ::= "PRIMARY" "KEY" | "SEMANTIC"
DataType              ::= "INT"
                        | "FLOAT"
                        | "BOOL"
                        | "STRING" "(" IntegerLiteral ")"

DropTableStmt         ::= "DROP" "TABLE" Identifier
DescribeTableStmt     ::= "DESCRIBE" "TABLE" Identifier
ShowTablesStmt        ::= "SHOW" "TABLES"

(* DML Statements *)
InsertStmt            ::= "INSERT" "INTO" Identifier "VALUES" "(" Value ( "," Value )* ")"
UpdateStmt            ::= "UPDATE" Identifier "SET" Assignment ( "," Assignment )* ( "WHERE" Condition )?
Assignment            ::= Identifier "=" Value
DeleteStmt            ::= "DELETE" "FROM" Identifier ( "WHERE" Condition )?

(* Query Statements *)
SelectStmt            ::= "SELECT" SelectList "FROM" Identifier
                          ( TemporalClause | WhereClause )*
                          ( "ORDER" "BY" Identifier ( "ASC" | "DESC" )? )?
                          ( "LIMIT" IntegerLiteral )?

SelectList            ::= "*" | Identifier ( "," Identifier )*
TemporalClause        ::= "AS" "OF" DateLiteral
                        | "SNAPSHOT" DateLiteral
                        | "BETWEEN" DateLiteral "AND" DateLiteral
WhereClause           ::= "WHERE" Condition

(* Temporal Inspection & Maintenance *)
CompareStmt           ::= "COMPARE" Identifier "WHERE" Condition "BETWEEN" DateLiteral "AND" DateLiteral
EvolutionStmt         ::= "EVOLUTION" Identifier "WHERE" Condition "BETWEEN" DateLiteral "AND" DateLiteral
HistoryStmt           ::= "HISTORY" Identifier "WHERE" Condition
RollbackStmt          ::= "ROLLBACK" ( Identifier "WHERE" Condition | "TABLE" Identifier ) "TO" DateLiteral
CompactStmt           ::= "COMPACT" "TABLE" Identifier "TO" DateLiteral

(* Conditions & Operators *)
Condition             ::= Identifier ( CompareOp Value | "SIMILAR" "TO" StringLiteral )
CompareOp             ::= "=" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">="

(* Literals & Values *)
Value                 ::= ( "-" )? ( IntegerLiteral | FloatLiteral ) | StringLiteral
DateLiteral           ::= DatePart ( TimePart )?
DatePart              ::= IntegerLiteral "-" IntegerLiteral "-" IntegerLiteral
TimePart              ::= IntegerLiteral ( ":" IntegerLiteral ( ":" ( IntegerLiteral | FloatLiteral ) )? )?

(* Lexer Terminals *)
Identifier            ::= [a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*
IntegerLiteral        ::= [0-9]+
FloatLiteral          ::= [0-9]+ "." [0-9]+
StringLiteral         ::= '"' [^"\\]* '"' | "'" [^'\\]* "'"

docs.title: Grammar Rules & Parser Invariants
docs.text:
1. Keyword Case-Insensitivity: All keyword terminals (SELECT, CREATE, TABLE, etc.) are matched case-insensitively.
  2. Clause Ordering in SELECT: The parser allows <TemporalClause> and <WhereClause> to appear in either order.
  3. Fixed Clause Ordering in Other Statements: In COMPARE and EVOLUTION, WHERE must strictly precede BETWEEN ... AND .... In ROLLBACK, WHERE must strictly precede TO.
  4. Single Condition Rule: The Condition rule supports exactly one comparison or semantic clause. No AND / OR boolean expressions are permitted within a WHERE clause.
  5. Date Formats: The TimePart rule supports hour alone (HH), hour and minute (HH:MM), and hour, minute, second with optional milliseconds (HH:MM:SS[.mmm]).

docs.title: The Embedding Pipeline
docs.text: This page describes how MemoraDB converts natural language text into 384-dimensional dense vectors using an in-process transformer model and Microsoft's ONNX Runtime.

docs.title: Model Architecture: all-MiniLM-L6-v2
docs.text:
MemoraDB embeds the sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model. This model is widely regarded as one of the best speed-to-quality trade-offs for embedding generation:

  • Base Architecture: MiniLM (BERT-style transformer architecture).
  • Layers: 6 transformer encoder layers.
  • Hidden Size: 384 dimensions (VEC_DIM = 384).
  • Parameters: Approximately 22.7 million parameters.
  • File Size: ~86 MB on disk (model.onnx).
  • Vocabulary: WordPiece tokenization with ~30,522 tokens (vocab.txt).

docs.title: The In-Process Inference Workflow
docs.text:
When text is submitted (either during INSERT/UPDATE or during a SIMILAR TO query), the MiniLmEmbedder executes the following sequence:

graph TD
    A["Input Text String"] --> B["WordPiece Tokenizer<br/>(Reads vocab.txt)"]
    B --> C["Token Tensors<br/>(input_ids, attention_mask, token_type_ids)"]
    C --> D["ONNX Runtime Session<br/>(Inference on model.onnx)"]
    D --> E["Last Hidden State Tensors<br/>(Batch x Seq_Len x 384)"]
    E --> F["Mean Pooling<br/>(Weighted by attention_mask)"]
    F --> G["L2 Normalization"]
    G --> H["Normalized float[384] Embedding"]

docs.title: 1. Tokenization
docs.text: The input string is broken down into subword tokens using WordPiece rules: * Special tokens [CLS] (start of sequence) and [SEP] (end of sequence) are prepended and appended. * Three 64-bit integer tensor buffers are constructed: input_ids, attention_mask, and token_type_ids.

docs.title: 2. ONNX Runtime Execution
docs.text: The tensors are passed to Ort::Session::Run: * Inference executes entirely within the memora process on the CPU. * No inter-process communication (IPC) or network requests occur.

docs.title: 3. Mean Pooling & Normalization
docs.text:
• Mean Pooling: The transformer's output token embeddings are averaged across the sequence length, taking into account the attention mask so padding tokens do not distort the representation.
  • L2 Normalization: The resulting vector is divided by its Euclidean norm, ensuring unit length (||v|| = 1.0). Unit length simplifies similarity calculations so that cosine similarity reduces directly to the dot product.

docs.title: Model Directory Resolution
docs.text:
At startup, MemoraDB dynamically discovers where the model assets live:

std::filesystem::path getModelDirectory() {
#ifdef _WIN32
    char* exePath = nullptr;
    _get_pgmptr(&exePath);
    return std::filesystem::path(exePath).parent_path() / "models" / "all-MiniLM-L6-v2";
#elif defined(__APPLE__)
    // Uses _NSGetExecutablePath
#else
    // Uses /proc/self/exe
#endif
}

This ensures that the DBMS executable can be launched from any working directory without breaking its access to the neural network weights.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
• In-Memory Retention: The ONNX session and model graph remain loaded in memory throughout the lifetime of the REPL session, eliminating model loading overhead on successive queries.
  • Embedding Latency: Generating an embedding on a modern quad-core CPU typically takes between 3 to 10 milliseconds per string.
  • Storage Footprint: Each embedding consumes exactly 1,536 bytes (384 floats x 4 bytes).

docs.title: How Semantic Search Works
docs.text: This page provides an end-to-end trace of how MemoraDB processes, scores, and ranks records during a semantic vector search query.

docs.title: Execution Pipeline
docs.text:
When you run a semantic query such as:

SELECT * FROM notes 
AS OF 2026-09-01 
WHERE body SIMILAR TO "deployment failure" 
LIMIT 5;

The engine executes the following six stages:

sequenceDiagram
    participant REPL as REPL / User
    participant Exec as Executor
    participant Temp as Temporal Engine
    participant Embed as ONNX Embedder
    participant VecIdx as VectorIndex
    participant VecTbl as vecTable
    participant Store as Table Storage

    REPL->>Exec: execute(SelectStmt)
    Exec->>Temp: generateCandidateKeys(mode=SNAPSHOT, t1)
    Temp-->>Exec: std::vector<VCandidate>
    Exec->>Embed: encode("deployment failure")
    Embed-->>Exec: float queryEmbedding[384]
    Exec->>VecIdx: semanticSearch(candidates, queryEmbedding, k=5)
    loop For each Candidate
        VecIdx->>VecIdx: findId(pk, timestamp)
        VecIdx->>VecTbl: readRecord(id)
        VecTbl-->>VecIdx: VecRecord
        VecIdx->>VecIdx: cosineSimilarity(query, target)
        VecIdx->>VecIdx: Push to Min-Heap (size <= 5)
    end
    VecIdx-->>Exec: Top-5 SearchResult objects (sorted desc)
    loop For each Result
        Exec->>Store: exactVersion(pk, timestamp)
        Store-->>Exec: Record (for column display)
    end
    Exec-->>REPL: ExecResult::Kind::SEARCH

docs.title: 1. Candidate Generation
docs.text:
The query's temporal mode determines which candidates to consider: * LATEST: Considers only the latest active version of each row (table.scanLatestKeys()). * SNAPSHOT / AS OF: Evaluates the anchor version active at t1 (table.snapshotKeys(t1)). * BETWEEN: Gathers all versions committed between t1 and t2 (table.selectBetweenKeys()).

Tombstoned (deleted) records are excluded from candidate generation.

docs.title: 2. Query Embedding
docs.text: The query string ("deployment failure") is passed to the MiniLmEmbedder. The in-process ONNX model produces a normalized float[384] array.

docs.title: 3. Cosine Similarity Calculation
docs.text:
For each candidate: 1. The engine calls VectorIndex::findId(pk, timestamp) to look up its 32-bit vector ID in the in-memory hash map. 2. vecTable::readRecord(id) seeks to id * sizeof(VecRecord) in <table_name>.vec and reads the 384-dimensional stored embedding. 3. The cosine similarity is computed: 

float cosineSimilarity(const float (&a)[VEC_DIM], const float (&b)[VEC_DIM]) {
    float dot = 0.0f, magA = 0.0f, magB = 0.0f;
    for (int32_t i = 0; i < VEC_DIM; i++) {
        dot += a[i] * b[i];
        magA += a[i] * a[i];
        magB += b[i] * b[i];
    }
    if (magA == 0.0f || magB == 0.0f) return 0.0f;
    return dot / (std::sqrt(magA) * std::sqrt(magB));
}

docs.title: 4. Top-k Ranking via Min-Heap
docs.text:
To maintain optimal memory and time performance, scores are managed with a min-heap priority queue (std::priority_queue):

auto compare = [](const SearchResult& a, const SearchResult& b) {
    return a.score > b.score; // Min-heap: lowest score at the top
};
std::priority_queue<SearchResult, std::vector<SearchResult>, decltype(compare)> heap(compare);

for (const auto& candidate : candidates) {
    // ... compute score ...
    if (heap.size() < k) {
        heap.push(result);
    } else if (score > heap.top().score) {
        heap.pop();
        heap.push(result);
    }
}
  • Complexity: O(N log k) where N is the number of candidates and k is the LIMIT. This is drastically faster than sorting all N candidates (O(N log N)).
  • Memory Footprint: The min-heap holds at most k elements at any time, requiring O(k) auxiliary memory regardless of how large the table grows.
  • Once all candidates are evaluated, elements are popped from the heap and reversed, producing a final list sorted from highest similarity to lowest similarity.

docs.title: 5. Result Decoration & Display
docs.text: For each result in the top-k list: * exactVersion(table, result.pk, result.timestamp) fetches the text values of all semantic columns from data.db. * The REPL formats the output into a clean table with columns: pk, timestamp, score, and <semantic_col>.

docs.title: Semantic Search Overview
docs.text: MemoraDB features an integrated, in-process semantic vector search subsystem powered by Microsoft's ONNX Runtime and the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 transformer model.

docs.title: Architectural Motivation
docs.text:
Most architectures requiring semantic search deploy a dedicated vector database alongside an existing relational database. This introduces substantial complexity: * Data must be synchronized between two distinct database systems. * Two network hops are required for each query. * Ensuring consistent transactional and temporal guarantees across both systems is challenging.

MemoraDB eliminates this overhead by embedding vector inference, vector persistence, and vector indexing directly inside the DBMS process:

graph LR
    A["SQL Query with SIMILAR TO"] --> B["Parser & Executor"]
    B --> C["In-Process ONNX Runtime<br/>(all-MiniLM-L6-v2)"]
    C --> D["Query Embedding (384-dim)"]
    D --> E["VectorIndex & vecTable"]
    E --> F["Top-K Ranked Results"]

docs.title: Key Components
docs.text: Component Implementation Description Model all-MiniLM-L6-v2 A 6-layer MiniLM transformer pre-trained on sentence similarity, outputting 384-dimensional vectors (VEC_DIM = 384). Runtime Engine Microsoft ONNX Runtime 1.22.0 High-performance in-process inference engine loaded via dynamic link library (onnxruntime.dll). Storage (vecTable) data/<table_name>/<table_name>.vec Dedicated binary file storing vector records (id, pk, timestamp, embedding[384]). Index (VectorIndex) In-memory hash index Maps {pk, timestamp} composite keys to vector IDs for fast retrieval. Search Operator SIMILAR TO SQL operator used in WHERE clauses to specify semantic query text. Ranking Algorithm Min-Heap Priority Queue Finds top-k highest cosine similarity scores in O(N log k) time.

docs.title: The SEMANTIC Column Modifier
docs.text:
To enable semantic search on a table, designate one or more STRING columns with the SEMANTIC modifier during table creation:

CREATE TABLE knowledge_base (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    title STRING(60),
    content STRING(500) SEMANTIC
);

Whenever a row is inserted or updated: 1. MemoraDB extracts the text from all SEMANTIC columns. 2. The MiniLmEmbedder tokenizes the text and runs the ONNX model in-process. 3. The resulting 384-dimensional float vector is written to <table_name>.vec.

docs.text:

  • Embedding Pipeline — Tokenization, model inference, and ONNX Runtime integration.
  • How It Works — Cosine similarity calculation, candidate generation, and top-k ranking.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The SIMILAR TO operator performs semantic similarity search on text columns declared with the SEMANTIC modifier. It converts the query text into a dense vector embedding, compares it against stored row vectors using cosine similarity, and returns the highest-scoring records ranked from most relevant to least relevant.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: SELECT * FROM <table> WHERE <semantic_col> SIMILAR TO "<query text>";

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
SELECT * | <columns> 
FROM <table> 
[ <temporal-clause> ]
WHERE <semantic_col> SIMILAR TO "<query text>"
[ <temporal-clause> ]
[ LIMIT <n> ];

[!NOTE] In SELECT statements, the temporal clause and WHERE ... SIMILAR TO can be written in either order: 

SELECT * FROM documents AS OF 2026-09-01 WHERE content SIMILAR TO "deployment error" LIMIT 5;
SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "deployment error" AS OF 2026-09-01 LIMIT 5;

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description <semantic_col> The name of a column declared SEMANTIC in CREATE TABLE. "<query text>" String literal containing the natural-language search query. LIMIT <n> Restricts results to the top <n> matches. If omitted, defaults to 10.

docs.title: 1. Basic Semantic Search
docs.text: SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "database crash recovery" LIMIT 3;

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
The output displays candidate records ranked in descending order of similarity score: 1. pk: Primary key of the matching record. 2. timestamp: Version timestamp of the record. 3. score: Runtime-computed cosine similarity score formatted to 4 decimal places. 4. <semantic_col>: The text content of the semantic column(s).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
pk    timestamp                score    content
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1     [Runtime Timestamp]      [Score]  A database stores structured information and implements WAL crash recovery.
4     [Runtime Timestamp]      [Score]  Operating systems manage computer hardware and handle system exceptions.
2     [Runtime Timestamp]      [Score]  The CPU executes instructions and performs arithmetic calculations.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3 result(s)

(Note: Exact similarity scores depend on the vector embedding generated at runtime by the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ONNX model).

docs.title: 2. Temporal-Semantic Search with AS OF
docs.text:
Find documents most similar to "compiler optimization" as the database existed last month:

SELECT * FROM documents 
AS OF 2026-08-01 
WHERE content SIMILAR TO "compiler optimization" 
LIMIT 5;

docs.title: 3. Temporal-Semantic Search with BETWEEN
docs.text:
Find historical versions from Q1 2026 that discuss "security vulnerabilities":

SELECT * FROM documents 
BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-03-31 
WHERE content SIMILAR TO "security vulnerabilities" 
LIMIT 5;

docs.title: How Scores are Interpreted
docs.text:
• 1.0000: Exact semantic match (identical meaning).
  • High Relevance: Strong conceptual overlap or close paraphrasing.
  • Moderate Relevance: Related technical concepts or shared domain context.
  • Low Relevance: Distant or unrelated topics.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The CREATE TABLE statement registers a new table schema within the MemoraDB catalog and initializes its on-disk storage files (data/<table_name>/data.db and optional vector tables).

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE <table> (
    <col1> <TYPE> PRIMARY KEY,
    <col2> <TYPE>
);

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE <table> (
    <col1> <TYPE>[(<size>)] [PRIMARY KEY] [SEMANTIC],
    <col2> <TYPE>[(<size>)] [PRIMARY KEY] [SEMANTIC],
    ...
);

docs.title: Parameters & Modifiers
docs.text:
Component Description Rules & Constraints <table> Name of the table. Up to 29 characters. Must be unique within the catalog. <col> Name of the column. Up to 29 characters. Column names must be unique within the table. <TYPE> Data type. One of INT, FLOAT, STRING, or BOOL. (<size>) Size specifier. Mandatory for STRING columns (e.g., STRING(50)). Must be a positive integer. Not permitted on INT, FLOAT, or BOOL. PRIMARY KEY Primary key constraint. Exactly one column per table must be designated PRIMARY KEY. SEMANTIC Vector embedding modifier. Valid only on STRING columns. Instructs the engine to generate 384-dimensional embeddings for text inserted into this column.

[!NOTE] Modifiers are order-independent: <col> STRING(100) PRIMARY KEY SEMANTIC and <col> STRING(100) SEMANTIC PRIMARY KEY are both valid.

docs.text:
CREATE TABLE students (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name STRING(50),
    gpa FLOAT,
    is_enrolled BOOL
);

docs.title: 2. Table with Semantic Search (documents)
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE documents (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    title STRING(60),
    content STRING(500) SEMANTIC
);

Created table 'documents' (3 columns) with semantic index

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Validation: The parser verifies column definitions, ensuring unique column names, a single primary key, and valid type sizing.
  2. Payload Calculation: Catalog::CalcOffset computes byte offsets for each column within the fixed-size row payload.
  3. Directory & File Creation:
  4. Creates directory data/<table>/.
  5. Creates data/<table>/archive/ for historical archives.
  6. Writes the binary TableMeta header into data/<table>/data.db.
  7. Semantic Vector Setup: If any column has SEMANTIC, vecMeta::createVecTable creates data/<table>/<table>.vec with header metadata.
  8. Catalog Registration: An in-memory Table instance is constructed and mounted into the catalog.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The DELETE FROM statement soft-deletes matching rows from a table. In MemoraDB, a deletion does not erase the row from disk; instead, it appends a tombstone record (deleted = 1) to data.db. The row is excluded from standard queries but remains preserved for historical and temporal inspection.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: DELETE FROM <table> WHERE <condition>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text: DELETE FROM <table> [WHERE <condition>];

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description <table> The target table name. WHERE <condition> Optional filter condition. If omitted, every active row in the table is deleted.

docs.title: 1. Delete Specific Row by Primary Key (students)
docs.text: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: 2. Delete with Comparison Condition (students)
docs.text: DELETE FROM students WHERE gpa < 2.0;

docs.title: 3. Delete All Rows (students)
docs.text: DELETE FROM students;

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text: 1 row(s) deleted

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Target Selection: The executor scans the current active records (table->scanLatest()).
  2. WHERE Filtering: If a WHERE clause is provided, matching records are identified.
  3. Tombstone Append:
  4. For each target record, table->deleteRow(pk) is invoked.
  5. A new record is appended to the end of data.db with the deleted flag set to 1.
  6. The new version {timestamp, offset} is added to HistoryIndex.
  7. Subsequent Query Behavior:
  8. Standard SELECT * FROM table; ignores tombstoned records.
  9. SELECT * FROM table AS OF <past_date>; will still return the record if it was active at <past_date>.
  10. HISTORY table WHERE pk = <val>; displays the complete lifecycle, including the tombstone event.

docs.text: Error Condition Error Message Table Does Not Exist No such table: '<table>' Unknown Column in WHERE Unknown column '<col>' on table '<table>' Primary Key Not Found If no active rows match the condition, 0 row(s) deleted is returned.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The INSERT INTO statement appends a new record to a table. Because MemoraDB is an append-only DBMS, every insert writes an immutable record stamped with the current system millisecond timestamp and creates the initial version in that row's version chain.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: INSERT INTO <table> VALUES (<v1>, <v2>);

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text: INSERT INTO <table> VALUES (<v1>, <v2>, ...);

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Description <table> The target table name. <v1>, <v2>, ... Positional values corresponding to every column in the table in the exact order declared during CREATE TABLE.

[!IMPORTANT] Values are strictly positional. You cannot specify a custom column subset or reorder columns in INSERT. All column values must be provided.

docs.title: 1. Insert into Relational Table (students)
docs.text: INSERT INTO students VALUES (1, "Alice Chen", 3.85, true);

docs.title: 2. Insert into Semantic Table (documents)
docs.text: INSERT INTO documents VALUES (1, "Architecture Overview", "MemoraDB is an append-only DBMS with temporal and semantic search.");

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text: 1 row inserted

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Column Count Check: Verifies that the number of values in the statement matches meta.columnCount.
  2. Type Validation: Validates that each literal conforms to the expected column data type (INT, FLOAT, STRING, BOOL).
  3. Primary Key Uniqueness: Extracts the primary key value. If HistoryIndex::contains(pk) returns true, the insert is rejected (primary keys must be unique).
  4. Append Record:
  5. Seeks to the end of data/<table_name>/data.db.
  6. Writes the 9-byte header: timestamp = current_time_ms() and deleted = 0.
  7. Writes the fixed-size row payload.
  8. Update History Index: Adds {timestamp, file_offset} to the table's in-memory HistoryIndex.
  9. Generate Semantic Vector: If the table contains any SEMANTIC column, the text from all semantic columns is concatenated and passed to the ONNX MiniLmEmbedder. The resulting 384-dimensional vector is appended to data/<table_name>/<table_name>.vec.

Value Exceeds String Size Rejection during row validation if string exceeds declared byte capacity. Embedding Generation Failure Failed to create ONNX embedding

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The LIMIT clause restricts the maximum number of records returned by a SELECT statement.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: SELECT ... FROM <table> LIMIT <n>;

docs.text: SELECT ... FROM <table> [...] LIMIT <n>;

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description <n> A non-negative integer specifying the maximum row count to return.

docs.title: 1. Relational Queries
docs.text:
In standard relational queries, LIMIT truncates the resulting vector of records to the first <n> rows after any WHERE filtering and ORDER BY sorting have been applied.

SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY gpa DESC LIMIT 5;

docs.title: 2. Semantic Queries (SIMILAR TO)
docs.text:
In semantic search queries, LIMIT sets the capacity k of the top-k min-heap: * If LIMIT is specified: Returns the top <n> most similar records. * If LIMIT is omitted: The semantic engine defaults to returning the top 10 records.

-- Returns top 3 most semantically similar documents
SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "network timeout" LIMIT 3;

-- Returns top 10 by default
SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "network timeout";

docs.text: The ORDER BY clause sorts query results by a specified column in ascending (ASC) or descending (DESC) order.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.text: SELECT ... FROM <table> ORDER BY <column>;

docs.title: Type-Aware Sorting Behavior
docs.text:
Sorting respects the underlying data type of the column:

  • INT Columns: Numerically sorted by parsed integer value (std::stoi).
  • FLOAT Columns: Numerically sorted by parsed float value (std::stof).
  • STRING Columns: Lexicographically sorted by character code points.
  • BOOL Columns: false sorts before true in ascending order.

docs.title: SQL Reference Overview
docs.text: MemoraDB provides a custom SQL-like query language designed specifically for its append-only temporal and semantic architecture.

docs.title: Dialect Characteristics
docs.text:
Before writing queries in MemoraDB, note the following language rules:

  • Keyword Case-Insensitivity: All SQL keywords are case-insensitive. SELECT, select, and Select are treated identically.
  • Identifier Case Sensitivity: Identifiers (table names and column names) are matched against schema definitions. The parser will attempt exact match followed by lowercase fallback.
  • Semicolon Termination: Every SQL statement must terminate with a semicolon (;). Statements without a semicolon will prompt the REPL for continuation lines (...>).
  • String Literals: Strings can be quoted using either single quotes ('text') or double quotes ("text").
  • Numeric Literals: Integers (42, -10) and floating-point numbers (3.14, -0.05) are natively supported, including unary minus.
  • No Inline SQL Comments: The MemoraDB lexer does not include comment tokens (such as -- or /* */). Do not include SQL comment markers in statements sent to the REPL.

docs.title: Supported Statement Categories
docs.text: MemoraDB organizes statements into four functional categories:

docs.title: 1. Data Definition Language (DDL)
docs.text: Statement Description CREATE TABLE Defines a new table schema with typed columns and primary key. DROP TABLE Deletes a table and removes its data directory from disk. DESCRIBE TABLE Prints the schema definition and column metadata of a table. SHOW TABLES Lists all tables currently registered in the database catalog.

docs.title: 2. Data Manipulation Language (DML)
docs.text: Statement Description INSERT INTO Appends a new row version with positional column values. UPDATE Appends a new row version with updated column values. DELETE FROM Appends a tombstone record marking rows as deleted.

docs.title: 3. Query Language (QL)
docs.text: Feature Description SELECT Reads records with projection (* or column list), ordering, and limits. WHERE Clause Filters records using comparison operators or semantic search. ORDER BY Sorts query results by a specified column in ascending or descending order. LIMIT Restricts the maximum number of records returned.

docs.title: 4. Temporal Statements
docs.text: Statement Description AS OF / SNAPSHOT Queries the state of a table as of a past date or instant. BETWEEN ... AND ... Queries all versions committed within a time window. HISTORY Displays the full version chain for a specific primary key. EVOLUTION Displays step-by-step column diffs across consecutive versions. COMPARE Displays net column differences between two points in time. ROLLBACK Restores a row or table to a past state by appending new records. COMPACT TABLE Purges superseded history prior to an anchor date and archives old data.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The SELECT statement queries records from a table. It supports column projection, row filtering (WHERE), point-in-time and time-interval temporal queries (AS OF, SNAPSHOT, BETWEEN), semantic similarity search (SIMILAR TO), result sorting (ORDER BY), and pagination (LIMIT).

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: SELECT * FROM <table>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
SELECT * | <col1>[, <col2> ...]
FROM <table>
[ <temporal-clause> ]
[ WHERE <condition> ]
[ ORDER BY <col> [ASC|DESC] ]
[ LIMIT <n> ];

Where <temporal-clause> can be: 

AS OF <date>
SNAPSHOT <date>
BETWEEN <date1> AND <date2>

[!NOTE] Flexible Clause Ordering in SELECT: The <temporal-clause> and WHERE clause are independent and can appear in either order: 

SELECT * FROM employees AS OF 2026-09-01 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE id = 1 AS OF 2026-09-01;
Both forms parse and execute identically in MemoraDB.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Component Description * Selects all columns in the table schema. <col1>, <col2> Explicit column projection. Only specified columns will be returned. FROM <table> The target table name. AS OF <date> / SNAPSHOT <date> Evaluates the table state as of the specified date or timestamp. BETWEEN <d1> AND <d2> Returns all record versions committed between d1 (inclusive start) and d2 (inclusive end). WHERE <condition> Filters records by a comparison (=, !=, <, <=, >, >=) or semantic similarity (SIMILAR TO). Only one condition is permitted per statement. ORDER BY <col> [ASC\|DESC] Sorts rows by <col>. Defaults to ASC if omitted. LIMIT <n> Limits output to the first <n> rows.

docs.title: Execution Branches: Ordinary vs. Semantic
docs.text: The executor routes SELECT into one of two execution paths based on the WHERE operator:

docs.title: 1. Semantic Search Branch (SIMILAR TO)
docs.text: When WHERE <col> SIMILAR TO "<text>" is used: * The column must have been declared SEMANTIC during CREATE TABLE. * The query string is encoded into a 384-dimensional vector using the in-process ONNX model. * Candidate records are filtered by temporal constraints (if specified). * Cosine similarity is computed against each candidate's vector. * A min-heap extracts the top-k highest scoring records (defaults to k = 10 if LIMIT is omitted). * Results display the primary key, version timestamp, similarity score (runtime-computed float), and semantic column values.

docs.title: 2. Ordinary Relational Branch
docs.text: When SIMILAR TO is not present: * Candidates are generated based on the temporal mode (LATEST, SNAPSHOT, or BETWEEN). * If WHERE is present, rows are filtered using the comparison operator. * If ORDER BY is present, records are sorted according to column data type. * If LIMIT is present, the result vector is truncated. * If specific columns were requested, rows are projected to include only those columns.

docs.title: 1. Standard Relational Query (students)
docs.text: SELECT id, name, gpa FROM students WHERE gpa >= 3.5 ORDER BY gpa DESC LIMIT 5;

docs.title: 2. Point-in-Time Temporal Query (employees)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM employees AS OF 2026-01-15 WHERE id = 101;

docs.title: 3. Range-Based Temporal Query (employees)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM employees BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-06-30;

docs.title: 4. Semantic Search with Limit (documents)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "database crash recovery" LIMIT 3;

docs.title: 5. Combined Temporal + Semantic Query (documents)
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM documents 
BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-06-01 
WHERE content SIMILAR TO "container orchestration" 
LIMIT 5;

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The UPDATE statement modifies column values for existing rows. In MemoraDB's append-only architecture, an update does not overwrite the existing bytes on disk; instead, it creates and appends a new version of each target row with an updated timestamp.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: UPDATE <table> SET <col> = <val> WHERE <condition>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text: UPDATE <table> SET <col1> = <v1>[, <col2> = <v2> ...] [WHERE <condition>];

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Description <table> The target table name. SET <col> = <v> One or more column assignments separated by commas. WHERE <condition> Optional filter condition. If omitted, every active row in the table is updated.

[!WARNING] Primary Key Immutability: You cannot update the primary key column. Primary keys serve as the immutable anchor for record version chains. To change a primary key, you must DELETE the record and INSERT a new record.

docs.title: 1. Update Specific Row with WHERE (students)
docs.text: UPDATE students SET gpa = 3.95 WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: 2. Update Multiple Columns (students)
docs.text: UPDATE students SET gpa = 4.00, is_enrolled = true WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: 3. Update Semantic Text Column (documents)
docs.text:
UPDATE documents 
SET content = "All microservices deployed cleanly to production cluster." 
WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: Expected Output
docs.text: 1 row(s) updated

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Target Identification: The engine scans the latest active rows (table->scanLatest()) and filters them against the WHERE clause (if provided).
  2. Assignment Validation:
  3. Validates that all target columns exist in the schema.
  4. Verifies that no assignment attempts to alter the primary key column.
  5. Validates each new value against the column's data type and size constraints.
  6. Append New Version:
  7. For each matched record, a new Row is constructed with the modified values.
  8. If the table contains a SEMANTIC column, a new 384-dimensional embedding is generated via ONNX Runtime.
  9. The new version is appended to the end of data.db (and .vec).
  10. The in-memory HistoryIndex registers the new {timestamp, file_offset} for that primary key.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The WHERE clause filters rows in SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE, and temporal statements (COMPARE, EVOLUTION, HISTORY, ROLLBACK). It supports relational comparison operators as well as semantic similarity search.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: WHERE <column> = <value>

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
-- Relational comparison
WHERE <column> (= | != | < | <= | > | >=) <value>

-- Semantic search (SELECT only)
WHERE <semantic_col> SIMILAR TO "<query text>"

Supported comparison operators:

Operator Meaning Applicable Data Types = Equal to INT, FLOAT, STRING, BOOL != Not equal to INT, FLOAT, STRING, BOOL < Less than INT, FLOAT, STRING <= Less than or equal to INT, FLOAT, STRING > Greater than INT, FLOAT, STRING >= Greater than or equal to INT, FLOAT, STRING

[!IMPORTANT] SIMILAR TO is supported only in SELECT statements, and only on columns declared with the SEMANTIC modifier in CREATE TABLE.

docs.title: 1. Single Condition Only
docs.text:
MemoraDB supports exactly one condition per WHERE clause. Compound logical operations with AND or OR chains are not supported:

-- Valid
SELECT * FROM students WHERE gpa >= 3.5;

-- Invalid: compound conditions are not supported
SELECT * FROM students WHERE gpa >= 3.5 AND is_enrolled = true;
-- Parse Error

docs.title: 2. Boolean Type Comparisons
docs.text: For BOOL columns, only = and != are valid. Relational ordering operators (<, <=, >, >=) evaluate to false for boolean fields.

docs.title: 1. Integer Comparison (students)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: 2. Floating-Point Comparison (students)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM students WHERE gpa >= 3.5;

docs.title: 3. String Comparison (students)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM students WHERE name = "Alice Chen";

docs.title: 4. Semantic Search (documents)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "SSL certificate expiration" LIMIT 5;

WHERE on a SEMANTIC column Invalid Operator Expected a comparison operator (=, !=, <, <=, >, >=) but got ...

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The AS OF and SNAPSHOT clauses reconstruct the state of a table as of a specific past date or instant. Both keywords are syntactically and semantically identical in MemoraDB.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: SELECT * FROM <table> AS OF <date>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
SELECT * | <columns> FROM <table> (AS OF | SNAPSHOT) <date> [WHERE <condition>];

[!NOTE] Flexible Clause Ordering: In SELECT statements, the temporal clause and WHERE clause can be written in either order: 

SELECT * FROM employees AS OF 2026-09-20 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE id = 1 AS OF 2026-09-20;

docs.title: Date-Only vs. Timestamp Semantics
docs.text: A critical detail in MemoraDB's temporal engine is how date literals are interpreted:

docs.title: 1. Date-Only Literals (YYYY-MM-DD)
docs.text: When you provide a bare date without a time portion (e.g., 2026-09-20), the engine interprets this as the end of that whole day (23:59:59.999). * This ensures that any records inserted or updated at any point during that calendar day are included in the query result.

docs.title: 2. Explicit Timestamp Literals (YYYY-MM-DD HH[:MM[:SS[.mmm]]])
docs.text:
When you provide an explicit time (e.g., 2026-09-20 00:00:00.000), the engine evaluates the snapshot at that exact millisecond instant.

-- Evaluates state at the END of September 20 (23:59:59.999)
SELECT * FROM employees AS OF 2026-09-20;

-- Evaluates state at the EXACT START of September 20 (00:00:00.000)
SELECT * FROM employees AS OF 2026-09-20 00:00:00.000;

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Date Parsing: The date string is parsed into a 64-bit epoch timestamp in milliseconds (Executor::dayEndMs).
  2. Anchor Version Lookup:
  3. For each primary key in the table, the engine calls HistoryIndex::latestBefore(pk, targetMs).
  4. Binary search locates the newest version created on or before targetMs.
  5. Tombstone Filtering:
  6. If the anchor version has deleted == 1, the row is treated as non-existent at that point in time.
  7. If deleted == 0, the record payload is read from disk at version.offset.
  8. WHERE & Projection: Any WHERE conditions, ORDER BY, LIMIT, and column projections are applied to the snapshot records.

docs.title: 1. Query Entire Table As Of a Past Date (employees)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM employees AS OF 2026-01-01;

docs.title: 2. Query Specific Row As Of an Exact Timestamp (employees)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM employees AS OF 2026-06-15 14:30:00 WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: 3. Using SNAPSHOT Keyword (employees)
docs.text: SELECT id, title FROM employees SNAPSHOT 2026-08-01 WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: Related Commands
docs.text:
• BETWEEN — Query all versions in a date interval.
  • HISTORY — View all versions of a specific record.
  • ROLLBACK — Restore a past state.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The BETWEEN clause retrieves all versions of records committed within a specified time interval [date1, date2]. Unlike AS OF (which returns only one snapshot version per row), BETWEEN can return multiple historical versions for each row that was modified during the window.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: SELECT * FROM <table> BETWEEN <date1> AND <date2>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
SELECT * | <columns> 
FROM <table> 
BETWEEN <date1> AND <date2> 
[WHERE <condition>]
[ORDER BY <col> [ASC|DESC]]
[LIMIT <n>];

[!NOTE] In SELECT statements, the temporal clause and WHERE clause can appear in either order: 

SELECT * FROM employees BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-06-01 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE id = 1 BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-06-01;

docs.title: Boundary Semantics
docs.text:
• Start Boundary (<date1>): Interpreted via dayStartMs. If no time is specified, it defaults to the beginning of the day (00:00:00.000).
  • End Boundary (<date2>): Interpreted via dayEndMs. If no time is specified, it defaults to the end of the day (23:59:59.999).

This ensures that writing BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-01-31 covers the entire calendar month of January from the first millisecond to the last.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Range Conversion: Converts both dates to millisecond timestamps t1 and t2. If t1 > t2, an error is returned immediately.
  2. Version Retrieval:
  3. For each primary key, Table::selectBetween(pk, t1, t2) locates the first version committed at or before t1 (anchor).
  4. Iterates through all subsequent versions whose timestamp <= t2.
  5. Skips records marked with the deleted tombstone.
  6. Filtering & Output: Applies any WHERE condition and column projections.

docs.title: 1. View All Row Changes Across a Quarter (employees)
docs.text: SELECT * FROM employees BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-03-31;

docs.title: 2. Track Single Row Revisions (employees)
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM employees 
BETWEEN 2026-06-01 AND 2026-06-30 
WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: 3. Combined with Semantic Search (documents)
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM documents 
BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-06-01 
WHERE content SIMILAR TO "authentication timeout" 
LIMIT 5;

docs.title: Errors & Edge Cases
docs.text: Error Condition Error Message Start Date After End Date BETWEEN range starts after it ends

  • HISTORY — View full version history for a specific row.
  • COMPARE — View net differences over an interval.
  • EVOLUTION — View step-by-step diffs over an interval.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The COMPACT TABLE statement prunes superseded historical versions older than a specified anchor date to reclaim disk space. To prevent accidental data loss, MemoraDB archives the pre-compaction data file before activating the compacted storage.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: COMPACT TABLE <table> TO <date>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text: COMPACT TABLE <table> TO <date>;

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description <table> Target table name. TO <date> The cutoff date or timestamp. Versions prior to each row's anchor at this date are purged from active storage.

docs.title: Example (employees)
docs.text:
COMPACT TABLE employees TO 2026-01-01;

Expected Output: 

Compacted 'employees'
(Or Compacted 'employees' (with vector table) if a semantic index exists).

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: Compaction proceeds in four atomic stages:

docs.title: 1. Anchor Identification
docs.text: For each primary key in the table: * Finds the latest version committed at or before the cutoff timestamp (anchor). * Retains the anchor version and all subsequent versions. * Versions older than the anchor are marked for exclusion.

docs.title: 2. Temporary File Generation
docs.text:
• Opens data/<table_name>/data.db.tmp.
  • Copies over the table metadata header.
  • Sequentially writes each retained record, recording new file offsets into a fresh HistoryIndex.
  • If a companion vector table exists (.vec), vt->startRewrite() and vt->copyRecord() mirror the process.

docs.title: 3. Safe Archival
docs.text:
• Moves the active data.db to: 
    data/<table_name>/archive/archive_<timestamp>.db
  • Activates data.db.tmp by renaming it to data.db.

docs.title: 4. Index Swap
docs.text: • Replaces the table's in-memory HistoryIndex with the newly computed contiguous index.

docs.title: Safety Guarantees
docs.text:
• Non-Destructive Archival: The pre-compaction database file is preserved in the archive/ folder.
  • Point-in-Time Integrity: Because the anchor version is retained, running AS OF <date> queries at or after the cutoff date remains 100% accurate.
  • Vector Table Synchronization: Vector embeddings are rewritten and compacted in lockstep with relational records.

docs.title: Related Commands
docs.text:
• ROLLBACK — Restore past row versions.
  • HISTORY — Inspect version counts before and after compaction.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The COMPARE statement computes the net field difference between the earliest version and the latest version of a row within a specified time range. Unlike EVOLUTION (which lists every intermediate change), COMPARE collapses intermediate edits and shows only the net changes between the start and end of the interval.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: COMPARE <table> WHERE <condition> BETWEEN <date1> AND <date2>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
COMPARE <table> WHERE <condition> BETWEEN <date1> AND <date2>;

[!IMPORTANT] Strict Clause Order: In COMPARE, WHERE must strictly precede BETWEEN ... AND .... Both clauses are mandatory.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description <table> Target table name. WHERE <condition> Filter condition identifying the target row (e.g., id = 1). <date1> Starting date or timestamp of the observation interval. <date2> Ending date or timestamp of the observation interval.

docs.title: Example (employees)
docs.text:
Suppose employee 1 had multiple updates between January and December: * Initial salary was 75000.0 * Mid-year salary changed to 95000.0 * End-of-year salary changed to 125000.0

Running COMPARE:

COMPARE employees WHERE id = 1 BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-12-31;

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Retrieve Range Records: Calls Table::selectBetween(pk, t1, t2).
  2. Select Endpoints: Selects the first version in the range (recs.front()) and the last version in the range (recs.back()).
  3. Field-by-Field Diff: Calls compareRecords(front, back, meta). If a field's value in front does not match back, a Difference record is added containing column, before, and after.

docs.title: Errors & Edge Cases
docs.text: Error Condition Error Message Range Start After End COMPARE range starts after it ends Missing WHERE or BETWEEN Parse error (after the WHERE condition in COMPARE). No Matching Rows No rows matched

docs.title: Related Commands
docs.text:
• EVOLUTION — View all intermediate step-by-step diffs.
  • HISTORY — View full version timeline.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The EVOLUTION statement tracks the step-by-step field changes of a row over a time interval. It compares each consecutive pair of versions within the specified range, producing a chronological changelog of what was modified, when it was modified, and what the previous and new values were.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: EVOLUTION <table> WHERE <condition> BETWEEN <date1> AND <date2>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
EVOLUTION <table> WHERE <condition> BETWEEN <date1> AND <date2>;

[!IMPORTANT] Strict Clause Order: In EVOLUTION, WHERE must strictly precede BETWEEN ... AND .... Both clauses are mandatory.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description <table> Target table name. WHERE <condition> Filter condition identifying the target row (e.g., id = 1). <date1> Starting date or timestamp of the observation interval. <date2> Ending date or timestamp of the observation interval.

docs.title: Example (employees)
docs.text: EVOLUTION employees WHERE id = 1 BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-12-31;

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
The output displays each modified column across consecutive version pairs: 1. Timestamp: Time when the change was committed. 2. Column: Name of the modified attribute (or Deleted if tombstone status changed). 3. Before: Value prior to the change. 4. After: Value after the change.

(Note: Timestamps reflect the actual system time when each modification occurred).

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Timestamp                Column               Before                    After
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Runtime Timestamp 1]    title                Junior Engineer           Software Engineer
[Runtime Timestamp 1]    salary               75000.00                  95000.00
[Runtime Timestamp 2]    Deleted              false                     true
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3 change(s) across 1 row(s)

In this changelog: 1. At [Runtime Timestamp 1], the title and salary columns changed from their initial values to their new values. 2. At [Runtime Timestamp 2], the row was deleted (the Deleted flag changed from false to true).

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Resolve Primary Key: The engine locates the row's primary key using the WHERE condition.
  2. Locate Start Version: Finds the anchor version active at t1 (latestBefore(pk, t1)).
  3. Sequential Pairwise Comparison:
  4. For each consecutive version pair (r1, r2) in the history log up to t2:
  5. Calls compareRecords(r1, r2, meta).
  6. For each column where values differ (or if deleted changed), creates a Difference entry stamped with r2.timestamp.
  7. Return Changelog: Returns the ordered list of differences to the user.

docs.title: Errors & Edge Cases
docs.text: Error Condition Error Message Range Start After End EVOLUTION range starts after it ends Missing WHERE or BETWEEN Parse error (after the WHERE condition in EVOLUTION). No Matching Rows No rows matched

docs.title: Related Commands
docs.text:
• COMPARE — View the net difference between the start and end points directly.
  • HISTORY — View raw versions without pairwise diff calculation.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The HISTORY statement displays the complete version timeline for one or more rows. It retrieves every record version ever committed to disk for the matching row, including the initial INSERT, subsequent UPDATEs, and any DELETE tombstone.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: HISTORY <table> WHERE <condition>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
HISTORY <table> WHERE <condition>;

[!IMPORTANT] A WHERE clause is required. You cannot execute a bare HISTORY <table>; without a condition.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description <table> Target table name. WHERE <condition> A filter condition identifying the target row (typically <pk_col> = <val>).

docs.title: Example
docs.text: HISTORY employees WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
The output displays each version in chronological order, showing: 1. Timestamp: High-resolution creation time (YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm). 2. Deleted: Tombstone flag (NO for active records, YES for deleted records). 3. Column values as they existed in that specific version.

(Note: Timestamps reflect the actual system time when each record was inserted or updated).

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Timestamp                Deleted  id   name           title              salary
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Runtime Timestamp 1]    NO       1    Elena Rostova  Junior Engineer    75000.00
[Runtime Timestamp 2]    NO       1    Elena Rostova  Software Engineer  95000.00
[Runtime Timestamp 3]    YES      1    Elena Rostova  Software Engineer  95000.00
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3 version(s) across 1 row(s)

In this output: * Version 1 represents the initial INSERT. * Version 2 represents an UPDATE that changed the title and salary. * Version 3 represents a subsequent DELETE (marked with Deleted = YES).

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Resolve Primary Keys: The executor evaluates the WHERE condition to find all matching primary keys.
  2. Retrieve Version Chains: For each primary key, Table::showHistory(pk) iterates through all RecordVersion entries in the HistoryIndex.
  3. Read Records from Disk: For each version, the executor reads the record from its byte offset in data.db and prints the formatted timestamp, tombstone flag, and column payload.

docs.text: Error Condition Error Message Missing WHERE Clause Parse error (after table name in HISTORY (WHERE is required here)). Unknown Column in WHERE Unknown column '<col>' on table '<table>' No Matching Rows No rows matched
