  • COMPARE — View net field differences between two points in time.
  • ROLLBACK — Restore a past version from history.

docs.title: Temporal Database Overview
docs.text: MemoraDB is architected from the ground up as an append-only temporal database. Instead of treating past data as an ephemeral byproduct destined to be overwritten, MemoraDB makes historical state an actively queryable, first-class dimension.

docs.title: How Temporal Data Works in MemoraDB
docs.text:
Every data modification (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) appends a new record version to the table's data.db file with a 64-bit millisecond timestamp (uint64_t timestamp).

Version 1 (Initial Insert)  ──►  Timestamp: T1 (Offset: 0x0080)
      │
      ▼ (UPDATE)
Version 2 (Salary Modified) ──►  Timestamp: T2 (Offset: 0x0120)
      │
      ▼ (UPDATE)
Version 3 (Title Modified)  ──►  Timestamp: T3 (Offset: 0x01C0)
      │
      ▼ (DELETE)
Version 4 (Tombstone)       ──►  Timestamp: T4 (Offset: 0x0260)

docs.title: The In-Memory History Index
docs.text:
To provide fast lookups without scanning the entire data.db file on every query, MemoraDB maintains an in-memory HistoryIndex:

  • Data Structure: std::unordered_map<std::string, std::vector<RecordVersion>>
  • Ordering: For each primary key, versions are stored in strictly increasing chronological order.
  • Point-in-Time Resolution: HistoryIndex::latestBefore(pk, timestamp) uses binary search (O(log V)) to locate the active record version as of any historical instant.

docs.title: Summary of Temporal Statements
docs.text: Statement Purpose Description AS OF / SNAPSHOT Point-in-Time Query Reconstructs the exact state of rows as they existed at a specific past date or instant. BETWEEN ... AND ... Interval Query Retrieves all record versions committed within a time window. HISTORY Full Timeline Displays the complete lifecycle of versions for a specific row. EVOLUTION Step-by-Step Changes Shows the sequential, pairwise field diffs between consecutive versions over time. COMPARE Net Difference Computes the net field differences between the earliest and latest versions in a range. ROLLBACK Non-Destructive Restore Restores past state by appending historical records as new versions. COMPACT TABLE History Pruning & Archival Purges superseded versions prior to an anchor date and archives old data safely. Date & Timestamp Literals Syntax Specification Syntax rules, precision levels (ms), and defaulting semantics for timestamps.

docs.title: Flexible Clause Ordering
docs.text:
MemoraDB allows combining temporal clauses with relational WHERE clauses in either order:

SELECT * FROM notes AS OF 2026-09-01 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id = 1 AS OF 2026-09-01;

Both queries parse and produce identical results.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The ROLLBACK statement restores one or more rows—or an entire table—to a historical point in time.

docs.title: Non-Destructive Append-Only Semantics
docs.text:
In traditional databases, rolling back implies undoing transactions by modifying storage or truncating logs.

In MemoraDB's append-only model, ROLLBACK is strictly non-destructive:

graph TD
    A["V1 @ Jan: Salary $75k"] --> B["V2 @ Jun: Salary $95k"]
    B --> C["V3 @ Dec: Salary $125k"]
    C -->|"ROLLBACK ... TO Jun"| D["V4 @ Now: Salary $95k (New Record)"]
  1. It does not erase, overwrite, or delete versions committed after the target date.
  2. It queries the version active as of the target timestamp (selectAsOf).
  3. It appends a brand new record with the historical payload, stamped with the current time.
  4. The rollback action itself becomes a documented event in the row's ongoing version history!

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: (See the Syntax Notation Guide for notation rules).

docs.title: Basic syntax
docs.text: ROLLBACK <table> WHERE <condition> TO <date>;

docs.title: Full syntax
docs.text:
-- Row-level rollback
ROLLBACK <table> WHERE <condition> TO <date>;

-- Whole-table rollback
ROLLBACK TABLE <table> TO <date>;

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Description <table> Target table name. WHERE <condition> Required for row-level rollback. Identifies the row(s) to restore. TO <date> The historical date or timestamp to restore state from.

docs.title: 1. Row-Level Rollback
docs.text:
Restore row 1 to its state as of September 1, 2026:

ROLLBACK employees WHERE id = 1 TO 2026-09-01;

Expected Output: 

1 row(s) rolled back

docs.title: 2. Whole-Table Rollback
docs.text:
Restore all rows in the table to their state as of January 1, 2026:

ROLLBACK TABLE employees TO 2026-01-01;

Expected Output: 

Table 'employees' rolled back

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
• Row-Level (Table::rollback(pk, ts)):
  • Calls selectAsOf(pk, ts) to retrieve the active historical record.
  • If a valid record is found, calls appendRecord(record).
  • Writes a new record header with the current timestamp and appends the payload to data.db.
  • Registers the new version in HistoryIndex.
  • Whole-Table (Table::rollback(ts)):
  • Iterates over all known primary keys in HistoryIndex.
  • Calls selectAsOf(pk, ts) for each key.
  • Appends each retrieved record as a new version.

docs.title: Errors & Edge Cases
docs.text: Error Condition Error Message No Row Existed Before Date Rollback of table '<table>' failed (no row had a version before the given timestamp) Missing WHERE in Row Form ROLLBACK without TABLE requires a WHERE clause Table Does Not Exist No such table: '<table>'

docs.title: Related Commands
docs.text:
• AS OF — Inspect historical state before rolling back.
  • HISTORY — Verify that the rollback created a new version.

docs.title: Date & Timestamp Literals
docs.text: This page defines the syntax, precision, validation rules, and defaulting behavior for date and timestamp literals in MemoraDB.

docs.title: Supported Formats
docs.text:
MemoraDB supports five levels of granularity for date and timestamp literals:

Format Pattern Granularity Example YYYY-MM-DD Date only 2026-09-20 YYYY-MM-DD HH Hour 2026-09-20 14 YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM Minute 2026-09-20 14:30 YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS Second 2026-09-20 14:30:45 YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.mmm Millisecond 2026-09-20 14:30:45.250

docs.title: Defaulting Rules
docs.text:
When partial time components are omitted, MemoraDB auto-fills missing fields with zeroes:

Input Literal Hour Minute Second Millisecond 2026-09-20 00 00 00 000 2026-09-20 14 14 00 00 000 2026-09-20 14:30 14 30 00 000 2026-09-20 14:30:45 14 30 45 000 2026-09-20 14:30:45.250 14 30 45 250

docs.title: Millisecond Formatting Rules
docs.text: If a fraction is provided after seconds: * It is normalized to 3 digits. * .5 becomes .500 ms. * .05 becomes .050 ms. * Longer fractions are truncated to 3 digits (e.g., .1234 becomes .123).

docs.title: Validation Ranges
docs.text:
The parser validates all date and time components:

  • Year: Any 4-digit integer (1900 to 9999).
  • Month: 1 through 12.
  • Day: 1 through maxDay, computed dynamically based on the month and leap year rules (isLeapYear(year)).
  • Hour: 0 through 23.
  • Minute: 0 through 59.
  • Second: 0 through 59.
  • Millisecond: 0 through 999.

If any component falls outside these ranges, the parser throws a descriptive ParseError indicating the line and column number.

docs.title: The Bare Date Rule in AS OF and SNAPSHOT
docs.text:
An intentional design decision in MemoraDB is how a bare date (YYYY-MM-DD with no time portion) behaves in point-in-time queries:

-- Evaluates state at the END of that calendar day (23:59:59.999)
SELECT * FROM notes AS OF 2026-09-20;

-- Evaluates state at the EXACT FIRST INSTANT of that calendar day (00:00:00.000)
SELECT * FROM notes AS OF 2026-09-20 00:00:00.000;
  • Rationale: When a user queries "as of September 20", they typically expect to see data that was created during that day. Evaluating at 23:59:59.999 includes all activity from that date.
  • If you specifically need the start of the day before any business activity occurred, specify the time explicitly as 00:00:00.000.

docs.title: Troubleshooting & Common Issues
docs.text: This guide addresses common build, configuration, and runtime issues you may encounter when working with MemoraDB and provides verified solutions.

docs.title: 1. CMake Defaults to NMake or Fails to Find Generator
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Error: Running 'nmake' '-?' failed with: no such file or directory or CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER not set.

Cause: On Windows, CMake defaults to Visual Studio or NMake if no generator is specified, but NMake is not in your PATH.

Resolution: Explicitly specify your installed generator: * If you have Ninja installed: 

cmake -G "Ninja" -S . -B build
* If you are using MinGW (gcc / mingw32-make): 
cmake -G "MinGW Makefiles" -S . -B build

docs.title: 2. Missing 64-Bit Architecture on Windows
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Error: Automatic ONNX Runtime download currently supports Windows x64 only.

Cause: CMake detected a 32-bit compiler environment or non-x64 CPU. Modern ONNX Runtime precompiled binaries require a 64-bit platform (x86_64 / AMD64).

Resolution: Ensure you are using a 64-bit compiler: * For Visual Studio: open x64 Native Tools Command Prompt for VS 2022. * For MinGW: use the UCRT64 or MINGW64 environment (C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin). * To provide your own pre-built ONNX Runtime build, set: 

cmake -S . -B build -DONNXRUNTIME_ROOT="C:/path/to/onnxruntime"

docs.title: 3. Model Asset Download Timeout (Hugging Face)
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Error: Failed to download model asset onnx/model.onnx during CMake configure.

Cause: Network restrictions, corporate firewalls, or proxy settings preventing CMake from downloading the transformer model from Hugging Face.

Resolution: 1. Manually download model.onnx and vocab.txt from Hugging Face all-MiniLM-L6-v2. 2. Create the destination directory and place both files inside: 

build/models/all-MiniLM-L6-v2/model.onnx
build/models/all-MiniLM-L6-v2/vocab.txt
3. Re-run CMake configure. It will detect the existing files and skip the download.

docs.title: 1. "embedding model ready (off)" on Startup
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Status Display: ● semantic vector search ready (off) ● embedding model ready (off).

Cause: The executable could not locate models/all-MiniLM-L6-v2/model.onnx or vocab.txt. MemoraDB searches for this folder relative to the binary's actual location on disk.

Resolution: * Ensure the models/all-MiniLM-L6-v2/ folder is placed in the exact same directory as memora.exe (or memora). * If running from PowerShell inside build/: 

Test-Path .\build\models\all-MiniLM-L6-v2\model.onnx

docs.title: 2. Missing DLL Error on Windows (onnxruntime.dll)
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Error: onnxruntime.dll was not found or system error code 0xc0000135.

Cause: The ONNX Runtime shared libraries are missing from the folder containing memora.exe.

Resolution: Copy onnxruntime.dll and onnxruntime_providers_shared.dll into the directory containing memora.exe: 

# If using CMake FetchContent:
Copy-Item .\build\_deps\onnxruntime-src\lib\*.dll .\build\

docs.title: 1. "Cannot UPDATE the primary key column"
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Error: Cannot UPDATE the primary key column '<col>' (delete and re-insert instead).

Cause: MemoraDB uses an immutable append-only storage model. The primary key anchors the version lineage of a record. Overwriting a primary key in place would break time-travel consistency across versions.

Resolution: Delete the record and insert a new record with the updated primary key: 

DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1;
INSERT INTO users VALUES (2, 'Alice');

docs.title: 2. "Table name exceeds 29 characters" or "Column name exceeds 29 characters"
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Error: Table name exceeds 29 characters or Column name exceeds 29 characters.

Cause: Fixed metadata headers define tns = 30 (Table Name Size) and cns = 30 (Column Name Size), allocating 29 characters for the name plus 1 byte for the null terminator (\0).

Resolution: Use identifiers up to 29 characters in length (e.g., user_profiles instead of user_application_account_profiles_table).

docs.title: 3. Parse Error on Compound WHERE Clause (AND / OR)
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Error: Syntax error when executing WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2.

Cause: MemoraDB's SQL dialect currently supports exactly one comparison condition per WHERE clause.

Resolution: Filter by the most restrictive condition first, or project and inspect matching records: 

-- Supported:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';

-- Unsupported:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' AND total > 100;

docs.title: 4. SIMILAR TO Fails on Standard Column
docs.text:
[!WARNING] Error: Column '<col>' is not declared SEMANTIC, so SIMILAR TO can't be used on it.

Cause: Vector similarity search requires pre-computed dense embeddings. Only STRING columns declared with the SEMANTIC modifier during CREATE TABLE have vector index tables generated.

Resolution: Recreate the table with SEMANTIC on the text column: 

CREATE TABLE articles (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    body STRING(300) SEMANTIC
);

docs.title: Corrupted Record Warning on Startup
docs.text:
[!NOTE] Diagnostic Message: Corrupted record encountered during recovery.

Explanation: A previous DBMS process was terminated abruptly (e.g., power loss, killed process) while writing a binary record to data.db.

Engine Behavior: MemoraDB automatically scans the binary log on startup. When an incomplete or corrupt record header is detected, the engine automatically truncates the file back to the last known valid record boundary using std::filesystem::resize_file. No committed records are lost, and the database remains in a consistent state.

docs.title: Tutorial: Complete Real-World Workflow
docs.text: This tutorial ties together all of MemoraDB's capabilities—relational constraints, append-only temporal tracking, and in-process neural vector search—by building an Engineering Incident & Post-Mortem Tracking System.

docs.title: The Scenario
docs.text: As an infrastructure team, you need a database that can: 1. Store production incident tickets. 2. Track how an incident was diagnosed and resolved over time. 3. Allow engineers to travel back in time to inspect exactly what was known at each hour of an outage. 4. Search historical incident post-mortems using natural language to quickly diagnose future issues.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Incidents Table
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE incidents (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    service STRING(30),
    severity STRING(10),
    summary STRING(500) SEMANTIC
);

docs.title: Step 2: Record the Incident Life Cycle
Initial Alert
docs.text: INSERT INTO incidents VALUES (101, "AuthService", "SEV-1", "Users experiencing HTTP 500 errors during OAuth login redirect.");

docs.title: Root Cause Identified
docs.text: UPDATE incidents SET summary = "Root cause identified as database connection pool exhaustion in the user authentication cluster." WHERE id = 101;

docs.title: Mitigation Applied
docs.text: UPDATE incidents SET severity = "SEV-2", summary = "Increased max connection limit to 500. Login latency stabilizing across all regions." WHERE id = 101;

docs.title: Incident Resolved
docs.text: UPDATE incidents SET severity = "SEV-3", summary = "Permanent fix deployed. Connection pool leak resolved in patch v2.4.1. Incident closed." WHERE id = 101;

docs.title: Step 3: Audit Incident Evolution
docs.text:
To understand how the diagnosis progressed during the post-mortem review:

EVOLUTION incidents WHERE id = 101 BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-12-31;

Output Structure: 

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Timestamp                Column     Before                                                  After
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Runtime Timestamp 1]    summary    Users experiencing HTTP 500 errors...                   Root cause identified as database conn...
[Runtime Timestamp 2]    severity   SEV-1                                                   SEV-2
[Runtime Timestamp 2]    summary    Root cause identified as database conn...               Increased max connection limit to 500...
[Runtime Timestamp 3]    severity   SEV-2                                                   SEV-3
[Runtime Timestamp 3]    summary    Increased max connection limit to 500...                Permanent fix deployed. Connection...
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5 change(s) across 1 row(s)

docs.title: Step 4: Time Travel with AS OF
docs.text:
What was the status and summary of the incident when it was first reported, before the root cause was discovered?

SELECT severity, summary FROM incidents AS OF 2026-01-01 WHERE id = 101;

(Or use the timestamp corresponding to the initial insert).

docs.title: Step 5: Semantic Troubleshooting for Future Incidents
docs.text:
Months later, another team experiences login failures and runs a semantic search to check if a similar issue occurred in the past:

SELECT * FROM incidents 
WHERE summary SIMILAR TO "database out of connections during authentication" 
LIMIT 3;

Output Structure: 

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
pk    timestamp                score    summary
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
101   [Runtime Timestamp 3]    [Score]  Permanent fix deployed. Connection pool leak resolved in patch v2.4.1. Incident closed.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1 result(s)

The team instantly discovers incident 101 and the resolution patch, cutting MTTR (Mean Time to Resolution) dramatically!

docs.title: Step 6: Summary of Capabilities Demonstrated
docs.text: In this complete workflow, you used: * Relational Schema: Enforced types and primary keys on disk. * Append-Only Immutability: Captured every phase of the outage without losing prior observations. * Temporal Auditing: Inspected the timeline using EVOLUTION and AS OF. * Deep Neural Search: Found historical incidents using natural-language concept matching rather than exact keyword guessing.

docs.title: Tutorial: Semantic Search
docs.text: In this tutorial, you will explore MemoraDB's native neural vector search capabilities by creating a knowledge base, inserting technical documentation, and searching for concepts using natural language queries.

docs.title: 1. Create a Semantic Table
docs.text:
Launch memora and create a table with a SEMANTIC column:

CREATE TABLE documents (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    category STRING(30),
    content STRING(400) SEMANTIC
);

Output: 

Created table 'documents' (3 columns) with semantic index

docs.title: 2. Populate the Knowledge Base
docs.text:
Insert five technical summaries into the table:

INSERT INTO documents VALUES (1, "Storage", "A relational database uses structured tables, primary keys, and transaction logs.");
INSERT INTO documents VALUES (2, "AI", "Neural networks and machine learning models discover latent patterns in large datasets.");
INSERT INTO documents VALUES (3, "Hardware", "The central processing unit executes binary instructions and manages hardware registers.");
INSERT INTO documents VALUES (4, "Cloud", "Container clusters enable scalable microservice orchestration and automated failover.");
INSERT INTO documents VALUES (5, "Security", "Public key cryptography ensures secure communication over untrusted networks.");

During each insert, MemoraDB's in-process ONNX model automatically computes a 384-dimensional vector embedding for the content column and writes it to data/documents/documents.vec.

docs.title: 3. Query Concepts Without Exact Keywords
docs.text: Let's test semantic similarity by searching for terms that do not literally appear in the records:

docs.title: Query 1: "Deep learning algorithms"
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "Deep learning algorithms" LIMIT 3;

Output Structure: 

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
pk    timestamp                score    content
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2     [Runtime Timestamp]      [Score]  Neural networks and machine learning models discover latent patterns in large datasets.
5     [Runtime Timestamp]      [Score]  Public key cryptography ensures secure communication over untrusted networks.
1     [Runtime Timestamp]      [Score]  A relational database uses structured tables, primary keys, and transaction logs.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3 result(s)

(Note: The score column displays the runtime-computed cosine similarity between your query embedding and each stored row embedding).

Record 2 is ranked first because its vector representation closely aligns with "deep learning" in the semantic embedding space.

docs.title: Query 2: "Deploying Docker in Kubernetes"
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "Deploying Docker in Kubernetes" LIMIT 3;

Output Structure: 

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
pk    timestamp                score    content
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4     [Runtime Timestamp]      [Score]  Container clusters enable scalable microservice orchestration and automated failover.
1     [Runtime Timestamp]      [Score]  A relational database uses structured tables, primary keys, and transaction logs.
3     [Runtime Timestamp]      [Score]  The central processing unit executes binary instructions and manages hardware registers.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3 result(s)

Record 4 is ranked first because the neural model projects concepts of containerization, clusters, and orchestration into the same neighborhood in the 384-dimensional vector space.

docs.title: 4. Re-Embedding on UPDATE
docs.text:
When you update a record containing a SEMANTIC column, MemoraDB generates a fresh embedding in real time:

UPDATE documents SET content = "Deep learning and convolutional neural networks revolutionized computer vision." WHERE id = 2;

Now re-run the search for "computer vision":

SELECT * FROM documents WHERE content SIMILAR TO "computer vision" LIMIT 2;

Record 2 will be returned at the top of the ranked results reflecting its new content!

docs.title: Tutorial: Student Database
docs.text: In this beginner-friendly tutorial, you will create a student records database, insert student profiles, filter and sort query results, perform updates, and delete records.

docs.title: 1. Create the Table
docs.text:
Launch memora and create a students table:

CREATE TABLE students (
    student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name STRING(50),
    major STRING(40),
    gpa FLOAT,
    is_active BOOL
);

Output: 

Created table 'students' (5 columns)

Verify the schema:

DESCRIBE TABLE students;

docs.title: 2. Insert Records
docs.text:
Insert four students into the table using positional column order:

INSERT INTO students VALUES (101, "Alice Chen", "Computer Science", 3.85, true);
INSERT INTO students VALUES (102, "Bob Martin", "Mechanical Engineering", 3.40, true);
INSERT INTO students VALUES (103, "Clara Gomez", "Computer Science", 3.92, true);
INSERT INTO students VALUES (104, "David Lee", "Mathematics", 2.95, false);

docs.title: 3. Query All Students
docs.text:
Retrieve the entire table:

SELECT * FROM students;

Project only the student names and GPAs:

SELECT name, gpa FROM students;

docs.title: 4. Filter with WHERE
docs.text:
Find all Computer Science majors:

SELECT student_id, name, gpa FROM students WHERE major = "Computer Science";

Find students on the Dean's List (GPA >= 3.8):

SELECT name, gpa FROM students WHERE gpa >= 3.8;

docs.title: 5. Sort with ORDER BY and LIMIT
docs.text:
Rank the top 2 active students by GPA:

SELECT name, major, gpa FROM students ORDER BY gpa DESC LIMIT 2;

Output: 

Clara Gomez  Computer Science  3.92
Alice Chen   Computer Science  3.85

docs.title: 6. Update a Record
docs.text:
Suppose Bob Martin improves his GPA to 3.65:

UPDATE students SET gpa = 3.65 WHERE student_id = 102;

Output: 

1 row(s) updated

Verify that the updated GPA is reflected:

SELECT * FROM students WHERE student_id = 102;

docs.title: 7. Delete a Record
docs.text:
Delete the inactive student record:

DELETE FROM students WHERE student_id = 104;

Output: 

1 row(s) deleted

Verify that David Lee no longer appears in the active student list:

SELECT * FROM students;

docs.title: 8. Historical Verification
docs.text:
Even though David Lee was deleted, his history is safely preserved in MemoraDB's append-only storage! You can inspect his past record at any time:

HISTORY students WHERE student_id = 104;

docs.title: Tutorial: Temporal Workflow
docs.text: In this tutorial, you will explore MemoraDB's temporal database features by tracking an employee's career progression, auditing salary changes, and rolling back state without data loss.

docs.title: 1. Create the Employees Table
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE employees (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name STRING(40),
    title STRING(40),
    salary FLOAT
);

docs.title: 2. Record Career Progression (Simulating Time)
docs.text:
Let's insert an initial employee record:

INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1, "Elena Rostova", "Junior Engineer", 75000.0);

After six months, Elena receives a promotion to Engineer:

UPDATE employees SET title = "Software Engineer", salary = 95000.0 WHERE id = 1;

A year later, Elena is promoted to Senior Engineer:

UPDATE employees SET title = "Senior Engineer", salary = 125000.0 WHERE id = 1;

docs.title: 3. View the Complete Historical Timeline
docs.text:
Inspect every version in Elena's version chain:

HISTORY employees WHERE id = 1;

Output Structure: 

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Timestamp                Deleted  id   name           title              salary
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Runtime Timestamp 1]    NO       1    Elena Rostova  Junior Engineer    75000.00
[Runtime Timestamp 2]    NO       1    Elena Rostova  Software Engineer  95000.00
[Runtime Timestamp 3]    NO       1    Elena Rostova  Senior Engineer    125000.00
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3 version(s) across 1 row(s)

(Note: Timestamps reflect the actual system time when each record was inserted or updated).

docs.title: 4. Query Point-in-Time State with AS OF
docs.text:
Query Elena's status as of an earlier point in time:

SELECT title, salary FROM employees AS OF 2026-06-01 WHERE id = 1;

(Note: If the date specified is prior to the first update, the original "Junior Engineer" record is returned).

docs.title: 5. Trace Step-by-Step Changes with EVOLUTION
docs.text:
Track each specific attribute change across her entire tenure:

EVOLUTION employees WHERE id = 1 BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-12-31;

Output Structure: 

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Timestamp                Column               Before                    After
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
[Runtime Timestamp 2]    title                Junior Engineer           Software Engineer
[Runtime Timestamp 2]    salary               75000.00                  95000.00
[Runtime Timestamp 3]    title                Software Engineer         Senior Engineer
[Runtime Timestamp 3]    salary               95000.00                  125000.00
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4 change(s) across 1 row(s)

docs.title: 6. View Net Changes with COMPARE
docs.text:
What was the overall net change from when she joined until now?

COMPARE employees WHERE id = 1 BETWEEN 2026-01-01 AND 2026-12-31;

Output Structure: 

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Column               Before                    After
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
title                Junior Engineer           Senior Engineer
salary               75000.00                  125000.00
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2 difference(s) across 1 row(s)

COMPARE bypasses the intermediate "Software Engineer" stage and displays the net delta directly.

docs.title: 7. Non-Destructive Rollback
docs.text:
Suppose an administrative error occurred, and we need to roll Elena's compensation back to an earlier state:

ROLLBACK employees WHERE id = 1 TO 2026-06-01;

Expected Output: 

1 row(s) rolled back

Now query the active record:

SELECT title, salary FROM employees WHERE id = 1;

Finally, inspect HISTORY employees WHERE id = 1;. You will see 4 versions! Version 4 contains the restored values, proving that no history was deleted or lost during the rollback.
